title: Cryo-EM and Coupled Spectroscopies Shed Light on Degradation Modes in Iridium-Catalyst-Powered Water Electrolysis Membranes for Hydrogen Generation
content: Hydrogen represents an important energy transport and storage medium, and water electrolysis is a promising avenue for its generation, as these systems have the ability to operate at high, varying current densities, allowing them to interface well with dynamic sources of energy like wind and solar, where spikes in energy input would not be captured by less responsive systems with a lower dynamic range [1]. Proton exchange membranes (PEM)– composed of a polymer membrane sheet coated on either side with platinum (cathode) and iridium (anode) catalysts – enable one of the most promising low-temperature water electrolysis techniques, offering advantages such as high electrical efficiency and low operation cost [2, 3]. However, the catalysts required for the acid environment in PEM electrolysis operation are expensive, so the challenges to understanding degradation mechanisms in these materials also represent a cost hurdle to the widespread implementation of water electrolysis technologies [4, 5].
